results.name: endpoint_target_yes_deficit
results.description: Yes rate for the endpoint targets 1 and 100 minus the overall yes rate; observed below null means people reject the extreme numbers 1 and 100 more than the model predicts, above means the model under-endorses them.

results.name: prime_set_prime_target_contrast
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples are all prime, yes rate for prime targets minus yes rate for non-prime targets; observed below null means the model over-produces prime-rule generalisation, above means people follow the prime rule more sharply than predicted.
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_target_contrast
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples are all prime, yes rate for prime targets minus yes rate for non-prime targets; observed below null means the model over-produces prime-rule generalisation, above means people follow the prime rule more sharply than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    pr = np.zeros(101, bool)
    for k in range(2, 101):
        pr[k] = all(k % a for a in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1))
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    ok = np.array([(s.count(",") > 0) and all(pr[int(x)] for x in s.split(",")) for s in uniq])
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = ok[codes]
    a, b = m & pr[t], m & ~pr[t]
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: extrapolation_direction_asymmetry
results.description: Among multi-example sets, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus yes rate for targets below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward (toward larger numbers) more than the model predicts, below means they extend downward more than the model.
results.code:
# name: extrapolation_direction_asymmetry
# description: Among multi-example sets, yes rate for targets above the largest example minus yes rate for targets below the smallest example; observed above null means people extend generalisation upward (toward larger numbers) more than the model predicts, below means they extend downward more than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    mm = np.zeros((len(uniq), 2)); multi = np.zeros(len(uniq), bool)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        mm[i] = [min(v), max(v)]; multi[i] = len(v) > 1
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = multi[codes]
    a, b = m & (t > mm[codes, 1]), m & (t < mm[codes, 0])
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: single_example_same_decade_contrast
results.description: For single-example sets, yes rate for targets in the same decade (same tens digit, 100 counted with 91-99) as the example minus yes rate for targets in other decades; observed above null means people generalise within the example's decade more than the model predicts, below means the model over-produces decade/proximity generalisation.
results.code:
# name: single_example_same_decade_contrast
# description: For single-example sets, yes rate for targets in the same decade (same tens digit, 100 counted with 91-99) as the example minus yes rate for targets in other decades; observed above null means people generalise within the example's decade more than the model predicts, below means the model over-produces decade/proximity generalisation.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",").to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    e = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).to_numpy()
    dec = lambda x: np.minimum((x - 1) // 10, 9)
    same = dec(t) == dec(np.maximum(e, 1))
    a, b = single & same, single & ~same
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: power_rule_consistent_target_yes
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all lie in one power-type rule (squares, cubes, powers of 2, powers of 3), yes rate for targets that also belong to such a shared rule; observed below null means the model over-generalises mathematical power rules (people endorse rule-consistent targets less than predicted), above means it under-generalises them.
results.code:
# name: power_rule_consistent_target_yes
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all lie in one power-type rule (squares, cubes, powers of 2, powers of 3), yes rate for targets that also belong to such a shared rule; observed below null means the model over-generalises mathematical power rules (people endorse rule-consistent targets less than predicted), above means it under-generalises them.
def test_statistic(df):
    rules = [set(k * k for k in range(1, 11)), {1, 8, 27, 64}, {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}, {1, 3, 9, 27, 81}]
    mem = np.zeros((len(rules), 101), bool)
    for j, r in enumerate(rules):
        mem[j, list(r)] = True
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    tab = np.zeros((len(uniq), len(rules)), bool)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        if len(v) > 1:
            tab[i] = [all(e in r for e in v) for r in rules]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    sr = tab[codes]
    m = np.any(sr & mem[:, t].T, axis=1)
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: multiples_set_rule_contrast
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples are all multiples of some k in 3..12 (largest such k), yes rate for targets that are multiples of k minus yes rate for other targets; observed below null means the model over-sharpens multiples rules (people discriminate rule members less), above means people follow multiples rules more sharply than predicted.

results.name: digit_sum_set_match_contrast
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share one digit sum, yes rate for targets with that same digit sum minus yes rate for targets with a different digit sum; observed below null means the model over-produces digit-sum generalisation (people do not favour same-digit-sum targets as much as predicted), above means people use digit-sum rules more than the model.
results.code:
# name: digit_sum_set_match_contrast
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share one digit sum, yes rate for targets with that same digit sum minus yes rate for targets with a different digit sum; observed below null means the model over-produces digit-sum generalisation (people do not favour same-digit-sum targets as much as predicted), above means people use digit-sum rules more than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    ok = np.zeros(len(uniq), bool); sval = np.zeros(len(uniq))
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        d = {sum(map(int, str(e))) for e in v}
        if len(v) > 1 and len(d) == 1:
            ok[i] = True; sval[i] = d.pop()
    dsum = np.array([0] + [sum(map(int, str(k))) for k in range(1, 101)], float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = ok[codes]
    same = dsum[t] == sval[codes]
    a, b = m & same, m & ~same
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: Among multi-example sets, yes rate for targets strictly closer to the first-shown example than to the last-shown example minus yes rate for targets strictly closer to the last; observed above null means people weight the first example (primacy) more than the model, below means they weight the last example (recency) more than the model.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: Among multi-example sets, yes rate for targets strictly closer to the first-shown example than to the last-shown example minus yes rate for targets strictly closer to the last; observed above null means people weight the first example (primacy) more than the model, below means they weight the last example (recency) more than the model.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    uniq = pd.unique(sets)
    codes = pd.Categorical(sets, categories=uniq).codes
    fl = np.zeros((len(uniq), 2)); multi = np.zeros(len(uniq), bool)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        fl[i] = [v[0], v[-1]]; multi[i] = len(v) > 1
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    d1 = np.abs(t - fl[codes, 0]); d2 = np.abs(t - fl[codes, 1])
    m = multi[codes]
    a, b = m & (d1 < d2), m & (d2 < d1)
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())
